Fight Club. Chuck Palahniuk's nineteen ninety-nine novel, later adapted into a film by David Fincher, in which an unnamed office worker befriends a charismatic man named Tyler Durden and together they found an underground fight club.

An insomniac corporate drone meets Tyler aboard a plane. Tyler is a soap manufacturer and radical ideologue who believes that modern consumer culture has emasculated men. Together they create Fight Club, an underground fighting ring where men reclaim a sense of primal masculinity against the dehumanization of corporate life. Fight Club metastasises into something far larger: a massive anarchist organization called Project Mayhem, orchestrating terrorism and infrastructure destruction across the city.

Throughout the narrative, the narrator believes Tyler is a separate person with independent agency, making decisions and controlling Project Mayhem's operations. But the climactic twist reveals the truth: Tyler Durden is not a separate person. He is the narrator's dissociative identity, created during a period of psychological breakdown and manifesting the ideology and violent impulses that the narrator has been unable to consciously acknowledge. During his blackout periods, the narrator has been acting out Tyler's agenda while remaining partially aware but unable to stop himself.

In the climax, the narrator must confront his unconscious desires and the violent acts he has committed without knowing it. The film inverts the power dynamics of the narrative itself. As the narrator is confronted with this revelation, we as viewers are forced to reconsider everything we have witnessed. The twist complicates the film's anti-capitalist ideology and explores toxic masculine identity and its pathology. Fincher's direction, famous for unreliable narrators and visual innovation, weaponizes this dramatic irony to devastating effect.
